title: Power in a single case multiple baseline design

Furthermore, the number of baseline and intervention phase measurement was similar or there were more observations in the intervention phase than in the baseline phase. The number of observations was at least two within each phase. The start moments per participant could be unique or overlap. When the start moments were unique all participants had different possible start moments. For example, when there were three participants, the number of start moments was four, and the total number of measurements was 30, the range of possible start moments could be 4, 5, 6, 7; 8, 9, 10, 11; and 12, 13, 14, 15 while in the overlapping situation the range of possible start moments could be 4, 5, 6, 7; 5, 6, 7, 8; 6, 7, 8, 9. Note that large overlap in start moments was chosen to capitalize on the effect of overlap.

We believe that the randomization test, when used correctly, is a very flexible and complementary tool to value the statistical reliability of single case study outcome. We emphasize the correct use, because there are some pitfalls that are easily overlooked but may seriously hamper the interpretation of the statistical test. In order to correctly using a randomization test in a multiple baseline AB design it is required that one carefully specifies the range of possible start moments of the intervention a priori and then randomly draw the start moment of the intervention. This is important because in the randomization test it is assumed that each combination can actually occur in reality and that each combination of start moments has an equal probability to be drawn. When one of those aspects is not the case, a correct interpretation of the p-value cannot be guaranteed. In practice it may not be easy to define the range of possible start moments a priori. Take, for example, the clinical context where the baseline observations are collected when people are on the waiting list for a therapy. In this case it may be impractical, and even unethical to define a range of possible start moments beforehand and randomly draw one. Furthermore, in several contexts it may be inadequate or even impossible to randomly decide the start moment of the intervention. This is for example the case where an intervention has to start just after the baseline has reached stability. In these situation the randomization test discussed in this manuscript should not be used.

steps.title: Define Design Parameters
steps.instruction: Establish the structural characteristics of the across-subjects multiple baseline AB design.

substeps.instruction: Determine the number of participants (N), typically between 2 and 12.
Set the total number of measurements per participant (e.g., 15, 30, or 60).
Specify the number of possible start moments for the intervention (k) per participant (e.g., 2, 3, or 4).
Define the ranges of start points for the intervention for each participant (e.g., for N=3 and 15 measurements, ranges could be [T5-T6], [T7-T8], and [T9-T10]).
Decide if the start moment ranges for different participants will overlap or be unique.

steps.title: Collect Data
steps.instruction: Administer measurements to participants following the AB design structure.

substeps.instruction: Collect baseline measurements (Phase A) for all participants.
Introduce the intervention (Phase B) to participants at the staggered start moments defined in the design parameters.

steps.title: Generate Randomization Distribution
steps.instruction: Create a distribution of the test statistic using the Koehler and Levin (1998) randomization procedure.

substeps.instruction: Identify all possible permutations of participants and their possible start moments of intervention.
For each permutation, calculate the mean baseline and intervention scores based on the specific start moments used.
Calculate the mean difference between baseline and intervention scores, averaged over all participants for every permutation.
Use these averaged mean differences to form the randomization distribution.

steps.title: Calculate Observed Test Statistic
steps.instruction: Compute the actual mean difference from the observed data using the specific start moments used during data collection.

steps.title: Determine P-Value
steps.instruction: Calculate the statistical significance of the observed effect using a one-tailed test.

substeps.instruction: Count the number of permutations in the randomization distribution that have an averaged mean difference equal to or more extreme than the observed averaged mean difference.
Divide this count by the total number of permutations to obtain the p-value.
If the total number of permutations is too large, a random sample of 400 permutations can be used to approximate the p-value.

steps.title: Evaluate Statistical Significance
steps.instruction: Compare the calculated p-value against the nominal Type I error rate (typically .05) to determine if the null hypothesis should be rejected.
